takeaway: Ellsberg watches each distributed process's messages and simulates protocol-consistent states, alerting when no allowed event ordering could have produced an outgoing message.
background: A distributed protocol may be verified while the service implementing it still contains safety bugs. Static refinement proofs constrain implementation style, while testing cannot cover every deployed execution.
villain: A black-box runtime checker cannot see a concurrent process's internal message-processing order, so naïvely matching an incremental trace to the protocol creates an exploding set of possible executions.
approach: Each distributed process is co-located with an Ellsberg instance that receives a faithful, ordered trace of sent and received messages but sees no internal state. The instance simulates a user-provided protocol state machine, maintaining states reachable by reordering pending receives and timeouts; an outgoing message is accepted only if some reachable inducing state could emit it. Breadth-first search, immediate application of reorder-insensitive events, and lookahead prune the search, while instances require no cross-node coordination.
impact: The authors argue that runtime protocol refinement checking can complement proof and testing by warning operators when a deployed implementation exhibits a message-visible safety deviation.

evaluation.overview: The authors reproduce protocol bugs, measure latency and throughput overhead, and measure checker throughput and notification delay on Etcd, ZooKeeper, and Redis Raft.
evaluation.implemented: A roughly 4,500-line prototype, mostly in Go with a Python specification-testing tool, plus DPI-specific message mappings and IPC trace collection added at the systems' network APIs.
evaluation.setting: Three- and five-node CloudLab clusters run balanced and read-heavy YCSB-derived workloads with 120 clients; each Ellsberg instance is limited to two cores and checks traces once per second.
baselines: The same distributed protocol implementation without a co-located Ellsberg process (System)

results.text: When the authors reproduced the listed Etcd, ZooKeeper, and Redis Raft protocol bugs, Ellsberg notified on each; the experiments also exposed an unreported Redis Raft reconfiguration bug.
results.locator: PDF pp. 12–13 and 20–22 (paper pp. 1315–1316 and 1323–1325); §6.2, Table 2, and Appendix §D

results.text: The authors' largest observed 99th-percentile latency increase was 10.7%, from 7.25 ms to 8.03 ms, for Redis Raft under the read-heavy workload.

The authors report that, with once-per-second checking, Ellsberg processed one second of leader trace in 30–700 ms and follower trace in 20–180 ms, producing notifications within 1.7 seconds in their evaluation.

limitations: The guarantee assumes a correct Ellsberg specification, a faithful incrementally ordered trace, shared fate with the checked process, fail-stop failures, and an asynchronous or partially synchronous non-Byzantine protocol with enough state-revealing messages for tractable checking. Ellsberg can only flag deviations visible in outgoing-message content or order; it cannot prove correctness or detect deadlock, livelock, stored-data corruption, or performance bugs.
phd_group_signal: This work reflects a verification-systems style that derives an online algorithm from formal protocol models, engineers state-space pruning, and validates it against real implementation bugs and deployment overheads.

claims.text: For each outgoing DPI message, Ellsberg uses breadth-first search over protocol states reachable from pending incoming messages and timeouts; it reports a violation when no reachable inducing state can produce that message.
claims.locator: PDF pp. 8–11 (paper pp. 1311–1314); §§3.4–3.5, Listings 3–4 and Figure 2

claims.text: Ellsberg assumes a correct specification, fail-stop rather than Byzantine failures, asynchronous or partially synchronous execution, shared fate, and a faithful trace with per-connection receive ordering and program-ordered sends.

The checker observes no process state and only detects a bug once the trace contains an outgoing message inconsistent in content or order; it neither proves the implementation correct nor covers bugs without such a message.
